beats.speaker: client
beats.text: "We got offered a real storefront — first one either of us has ever had. I told the landlord I'd need to check with my partner before saying yes to anything."

options.text: Could you have said yes yourself, right there?
Of course you needed to check — obviously.
Why would a landlord care about your partnership at all?

beats.speaker: client
beats.text: "...Yeah. Technically. I just always run it by him first, out of habit at this point."

beats.speaker: reader
beats.text: You turn over the top card.

options.text: That's a habit, not a rule — the chain's loose enough to lift off whenever you actually try.
That settles it — the partnership needs to end.
This card has nothing to do with your business partner.

elaboration: The Devil's chains only look fastened — the card actually shows them loose enough to remove, which makes the checking-in you've built into every decision more habit than binding rule.

beats.speaker: client
beats.text: "So you're saying the partnership itself is the problem?"

options.text: No — it's not against the attachment itself, it's asking which habit is actually keeping you stuck.
Yes — cut him loose before it gets worse.
The card doesn't have an opinion on any of this.

elaboration: This is the most misunderstood card in the deck for a reason — it isn't purely bad, it just wants you to name the exact dependency or habit doing the holding.

beats.speaker: client
beats.text: "...Okay. Next time something like this comes up, I'm answering it myself first, and telling him after."
